chapter_title: Introduction to Roblox Studio and Your First Project
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the exciting world of Roblox game development! Our journey begins with Roblox Studio, the powerful, free-to-use development environment where all Roblox games are created. Think of Roblox Studio as your digital workshop, equipped with all the tools you'll need to design, build, and script immersive experiences for millions of players worldwide. It's a comprehensive platform that integrates 3D modeling, scripting (using Lua), animation, testing, and publishing all in one place. Whether you're aiming to build a complex role-playing game, a challenging obby (obstacle course), or a simple hangout spot, Roblox Studio is your starting point.

To get started, your first step is to download and install Roblox Studio. You can find the installer directly from the Roblox website (create.roblox.com). It's available for both Windows and macOS, and the installation process is straightforward, much like installing any other application. Ensure your computer meets the minimum system requirements, which are generally quite modest, but a decent graphics card and processor will provide a smoother experience, especially as your games become more complex. Once installed, you'll launch Studio and be prompted to log in with your Roblox account. This links your development environment directly to your Roblox profile, allowing you to publish and manage your creations. A common mistake beginners make is trying to launch Studio without an active internet connection or a valid Roblox account; ensure both are in order for a seamless start.

Upon successful login, you'll be greeted by the Roblox Studio home screen. This screen provides options to open recent projects, start new ones from templates, and access learning resources. For our very first project, we'll select a simple template to get acquainted with the interface. The "Baseplate" template is an excellent choice, as it provides a flat, empty canvas – essentially just a large, grey ground part – giving you maximum freedom to build from scratch. Other templates like "Classic Obby" or "Village" offer pre-built structures that can be explored and modified, but for learning the basics, Baseplate is ideal. Once you select a template, Studio will load your new workspace.

Now, let's take a moment to survey the Roblox Studio interface. It might seem a bit overwhelming at first, but we'll break down the most crucial panels. On the left side, you'll typically find the **Explorer** window. This is like a hierarchical file system for everything in your game. Every part, script, light, and player character exists as an "object" in the Explorer. Selecting an object here will highlight it in the 3D **Viewport** (the central area where you see your game world) and update the **Properties** window, usually located on the right. The Properties window is where you can modify the attributes of any selected object – its color, size, position, transparency, and much more. Below the Explorer, you'll often see the **Toolbox**, which is a marketplace for pre-made assets, models, and plugins shared by the Roblox community. We'll dive deeper into the Toolbox in a later chapter. The top ribbon contains various tabs like "Home," "Model," "Test," and "View," each offering a suite of tools for building, testing, and customizing your development environment. Don't worry about memorizing every button right now; we'll explore them as needed.

After creating your project and getting a feel for the layout, it's crucial to understand how to save and publish your work. Saving your game regularly is paramount to avoid losing progress. You can save your game to your computer as a `.rbxl` file (Roblox place file) using `File > Save to File As...`. However, to make your game accessible to yourself from any device or to eventually share it with others, you need to publish it to Roblox. Use `File > Publish to Roblox As...`. This will upload your game to the Roblox cloud, linking it to your account. When publishing for the first time, you'll be prompted to create a new game, giving it a name, description, and setting its privacy (e.g., private for development, public when ready). For now, always publish your game as "Private." This ensures only you can access it, allowing you to test and develop without public interference. You can always update a previously published game by selecting `File > Publish to Roblox`. Remember, saving locally and publishing to Roblox are distinct actions, both important for different reasons.

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how to set up Roblox Studio and create your first project. Roblox Studio is the integrated development environment where you build 3D worlds, add scripts, and test gameplay. We’ll start by installing and launching Studio, confirm you can log in with a Roblox account, and then create a simple Baseplate project that gives you a clean canvas to explore. Along the way you’ll meet the essential panels — the Viewport where you see your world, the Explorer that lists every object, the Properties panel that controls attributes, and the Toolbox where community assets live. You’ll also practice saving locally as an. rbxl file and publishing your project privately to the Roblox cloud so you can return to it from another device. I’ll emphasize common beginner mistakes — like attempting to open Studio offline or forgetting to publish — and show how to avoid them. By the end, you’ll have a private, published place linked to your account and a checklist to keep your work safe. Ready to begin building your first game workshop?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills you can use immediately. First, you will reliably install Roblox Studio and confirm it launches on your computer. That matters because a correct install avoids frustrating errors later. Second, you will identify and use the core UI panels: Viewport, Explorer, Properties, and Toolbox. Understanding these panels is essential to find where objects live and how to change them. Third, you will create a new project from the Baseplate template and know why that template is useful for beginners — it gives a neutral starting canvas. Fourth, you will save your work locally as an. rbxl file and publish the place to the Roblox cloud as Private. Publishing makes your project accessible from other devices and sets up future testing. Each objective includes a short practice so you can verify success: install and open Studio, click Baseplate, inspect a Part's properties, save to file, and publish privately. If any step fails, a short troubleshooting checklist will help diagnose common causes like missing internet or an unsigned account. These skills set a foundation for building and sharing your first Roblox game.

screens.title: Installing Roblox Studio
screens.subtitle: Download, install, and validate the Studio application

narration.text: Installing Roblox Studio is your very first practical step. Start by obtaining the installer from the official Roblox site and running it for your operating system. The installer guides you through standard steps like agreeing to terms and choosing an install location. After installation, open Studio and sign in with your Roblox account; this links your Studio environment to your profile so you can publish and manage your places. A concrete example: after running the installer and launching Studio, you should see the Studio home screen with options to create new projects or open recent ones. A common misconception is that Studio works entirely offline — while you can edit some local files, initial login and publishing require an internet connection. If the installer fails, check that any antivirus software isn't blocking it and that your system meets basic graphical requirements. Key takeaway: verify success by launching Studio and seeing the home screen while signed in. Try this immediate verification: open Studio, take note of the home page, and ensure the account avatar or name appears, confirming a linked account.

keyIdea.text: Run the official installer, launch Studio, and confirm you are signed in to access publishing features.

narration.text: Launching Roblox Studio and signing in connects your edits to your Roblox account and enables publishing. When you open Studio the first time after installation, the Home screen appears. This view shows templates, recent projects, and links to learning resources. Sign in with your Roblox account credentials so the environment can associate any published places with your profile. A concrete example: after you sign in, the Home screen commonly displays your username or avatar, and the "My Games" area will list places you’ve published. A common misconception is that saving locally replaces the need to publish; it does not. Publishing requires account linkage and an internet connection. If sign-in fails, confirm your account credentials and network connection. If you use two-step verification on your account, follow that flow when prompted. Key takeaway: before you create a new place, ensure Studio shows your account on the Home screen — this is the minimal confirmation you are ready to publish and manage game places. screens.title: Home Screen Templates — Why Choose Baseplate
screens.subtitle: Compare Baseplate with pre-built templates and choose what fits a beginner

narration.text: When starting a new place, Studio offers template options. For beginners the Baseplate template is recommended because it provides a minimal, flat ground and no extra models or scripts. In contrast, templates like Classic Obby or Village include pre-built structures and gameplay elements that can be useful for learning specific mechanics but also add complexity. A concrete example: Baseplate shows a single large flat part in the Viewport; selecting that part in Explorer reveals its properties in the Properties panel. Many beginners are tempted to pick a ready-made template thinking it will be faster; the misconception is that templates always save time. In reality, pre-built templates can hide important relationships between objects and scripts, making it harder to learn the basics. Key takeaway: choose Baseplate to learn core workflows with a clean canvas, and only explore more complex templates when you want to study how built games are structured. When to use: explore after you understand basic panels and object relationships.
Key Takeaway
Start with Baseplate to learn the environment clearly. Use templates later to study real project structure.

screens.title: Explorer and Viewport
screens.subtitle: How objects are organized and how selection maps to the 3D view

narration.text: Two central pieces of Studio are the Explorer and the Viewport. The Explorer is a hierarchical list of every object in your place — parts, models, scripts, lights, and services. Think of it like a file tree: Workspace contains the visible parts, and each part or model lives under Workspace. The Viewport is the rendered 3D scene where you move, rotate, and inspect parts visually. Together they form a linked system: selecting an object in the Explorer highlights it in the Viewport and updates the Properties panel. A concrete example: after creating a Baseplate, you’ll find Workspace → Baseplate in Explorer; clicking it in the Explorer will highlight the flat part in the Viewport so you can drag or scale it. A common misconception is that visible changes in the Viewport don’t affect Explorer — in fact, renaming, grouping, or parenting parts in the Viewport changes their arrangement in Explorer. Key takeaway: use Explorer to find objects by name and the Viewport to manipulate them visually. Practice selecting objects in both places to see the linkage clearly. Explorer and Viewport means explorer lists objects hierarchically; viewport displays and allows manipulation. selecting in one updates the other.. In practical terms, how objects are organized and how selection maps to the 3d view. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Misconception: changes in Viewport are separate; in truth, moving or renaming parts in the Viewport updates Explorer immediately.

Practice: click a part in Viewport and watch its node highlight in Explorer — this verifies the link.
Key Takeaway: Explorer helps you find objects, Viewport helps you manipulate them; use both together for efficient workflows.

screens.title: Properties and Toolbox
screens.subtitle: Modify object attributes and reuse community assets

narration.text: The Properties panel and the Toolbox are two complementary features you’ll use frequently. Properties displays attributes of any selected object — for a Part you’ll see values like Size, Position, Color, Material, and Transparency. Editing these fields changes the selected object immediately. The Toolbox is a repository of community-created models, assets, and plugins that you can insert into your place. A concrete example: select Baseplate and change the Material property to see how it affects appearance. Then open the Toolbox and search for a bench model to insert and place beside the Baseplate. A common beginner mistake is treating Toolbox items as trusted code; community assets can include complex models or scripts, so inspect them in Explorer and Properties before relying on them. Key takeaway: use Properties to control exact attributes and use Toolbox assets as starting points — always inspect inserted assets to understand their structure and scripts. Properties and Toolbox means properties controls object attributes. toolbox provides reusable assets, which should be inspected after insertion.. In practical terms, modify object attributes and reuse community assets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: The Ribbon and Useful Tabs
screens.subtitle: Home, Model, Test, and View — tools for building and testing

narration.text: The Ribbon across the top of Studio organizes tools into tabs like Home, Model, Test, and View. Each tab collects actions to support specific tasks. Home contains common actions such as selecting tools and inserting parts. Model offers geometry and alignment tools for building structures. Test provides play and simulation controls so you can run the place inside Studio to check behavior. View lets you show or hide panels and customize the editor layout. A concrete example: use Home to insert a new Part, then switch to Model to use the scale tool and snap alignment. Then go to Test to play the scene and verify that the part behaves physically. A common mistake is trying to test game logic without using Test mode — many interactive features only run when the place is simulated. Key takeaway: learn which tab holds the tool you need and practice the sequence: insert → modify → test. This routine keeps development focused and reduces trial-and-error frustration. The Ribbon and Useful Tabs means use home to add parts, model to edit geometry, test to play, and view to manage panels and layout.. In practical terms, home, model, test, and view — tools for building and testing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Saving Locally as .rbxl
screens.subtitle: Why to save locally and how .rbxl files work for backups

narration.text: Saving your place locally creates a. rbxl file that is a snapshot of the current workspace on your machine. This local save is important for quick backups and for keeping copies offline. Use File → Save to File As to write an. rbxl file to a folder on your computer; give it a meaningful name like MyFirstRobloxGame. rbxl so you can find it later. A concrete example: save after you place custom parts and change materials — if Studio crashes, you can reopen the. rbxl file to restore your work. A frequent misconception is that local saves replace the need to publish — they do not. Publishing uploads your place to the Roblox cloud and links it to your account, enabling cross-device access and testing in the Roblox client. Key takeaway: save locally often while you work, and also publish regularly. Treat local. rbxl files as versioned checkpoints you can revert to if needed. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Save to .rbxl

screens.title: Publishing Your First Game (Private)
screens.subtitle: Upload a place to Roblox and set privacy to Private

narration.text: Publishing moves your local place to the Roblox cloud so it’s associated with your account and can be opened from other devices or tested in the Roblox client. Use File → Publish to Roblox As to upload a new game. When publishing for the first time choose Create New Game, provide a name and brief description, and set Privacy to Private. Setting privacy to Private ensures only you can access the place while you develop it. A concrete example: name the place My First Cohortia Project and choose Private; once created, your place will appear under My Games in Studio. A common mistake is publishing as Public by accident — always check the privacy setting before finishing. Key takeaway: publish early and privately to protect unfinished work and enable cross-device development. After publishing, close and reopen Studio and confirm the new game appears in My Games to verify the process succeeded. Publishing Your First Game (Private) means use publish to roblox as → create new game, name it, and set privacy to private to protect your in-progress work.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Publish to Roblox
Publish Steps
1. Choose File → Publish to Roblox As.
2. Click Create New Game and enter a name and description.
3. Set Privacy to Private for development, then click Create Game.
4. Confirm the place appears under My Games in Studio after reopening.

Key Takeaway
Publishing privately preserves your development state in the cloud and enables testing across devices while keeping the place hidden from the public.

screens.title: Common Initial Setup Challenges
screens.subtitle: Troubleshooting installer, login, and publishing issues

narration.text: Beginners frequently encounter a handful of setup issues when first using Studio. The three most common are: installer blocked or failed, inability to sign in, and publishing errors. If the installer is blocked, check security software and re-run the installer. If login fails, verify your credentials and network connection; also watch for two-step verification flows. Publishing errors often occur when privacy is set incorrectly or when your account hasn’t been linked properly; always confirm the Create New Game dialog shows your account and that Privacy is set to Private. A concrete example: if publish fails with a message about account permission, sign out and sign back in, then retry Publish to Roblox As. narration.text: These three concepts form the foundation of your first Roblox Studio workflow. First, Roblox Studio: the integrated environment where you build 3D worlds, write scripts, and test gameplay. It bundles visual editing and scripting tools you will use together. Second, Explorer and Properties: Explorer lists every object hierarchically and Properties gives you control over attributes like size, position, color, and material. Selecting an object reveals its properties so you can edit them precisely. Third, Save versus Publish: saving to an. rbxl file stores a local snapshot, while publishing uploads your place to the Roblox cloud and links it to your account. Save frequently for backups; publish privately when you want cross-device access or to test in the Roblox client.
